--------
Denvonta “Dirt Rocc” Lee sits down with Vlad to revisit a tense moment he says he witnessed around Diddy, then known as Puffy, and The Notorious B.I.G. at the MGM around the time of the McNeeley fight. Dirt Rock recalls Biggie interrupting while Diddy was speaking and says Diddy warned him he would slap him, though he clarifies no physical slap happened.  

The conversation also moves through Compton street politics, including Mob Piru, Southside Crips, Suge Knight, Big Dre, and the longstanding neighborhood tensions between different sides of the city. Dirt Rock discusses sharing spots in Paramount and Hawthorne, his close relationship with Dre, and his memories of Orlando “Baby Lane” Anderson. He also responds to accounts involving Detective Lad, Blondie, and past shooting investigations where Anderson was reportedly investigated but not convicted. A firsthand look at hip-hop history, Los Angeles gang culture, and the Bad Boy era.

recentItems.title: Robert O'Neill: We Were Allowed to Kill 23 Civilians to Kill 1 Terrorist (Part 2)
recentItems.description:
Become a VladStocks Member now: https://www.youtube.com/vladtv/join

Part 1: https://youtu.be/2-Bi3FMDiz4
--------
Robert O’Neill joins Vlad and Nicholas Irving for a blunt discussion on rules of engagement, civilian casualties, and the moral limits of modern warfare. Reacting to an Israeli documentary about an alleged AI targeting system used after the October 7 Hamas attack, O’Neill questions whether algorithms should help decide how many civilians may die to eliminate one terrorist, while noting Benjamin Netanyahu has disputed the film’s claims.

O’Neill revisits Iraq in 2007, including missions around al-Asad, Fallujah, Baghdad, and Baqubah, where he says U.S. forces once operated under a roughly 23-to-1 collateral damage threshold. He contrasts targeted house raids with airstrikes, recalls President Obama’s guidance before the Osama bin Laden raid, and explains how changing battlefield rules affected troops on the ground. Irving adds a sniper’s perspective from early Iraq as they discuss SEAL Team Six, Rangers, Delta Force, AI warfare, and the realities behind combat decisions.

--------

Trap Lore Ross sits down with VladTV to unpack the fallout from Lil Durk’s federal trial, clarifying why he said Durk’s defense “blamed” OTF Vonnie—not that Durk cooperated or snitched. Ross details the courtroom debate over opening arguments, King Von, Little Pab, alleged cartel claims, and the viral Brian Steel AI meme that took over social media after the verdict. He also addresses being confronted outside court, 6ix9ine amplifying the snitching narrative, and why the “snitch jacket” conversation remains so disputed in hip-hop culture.

The discussion turns to OTF Vonnie and OTF Jam, who Ross says are now in an ugly position after Durk beat five counts while still facing two unresolved charges. DJ Vlad and Ross revisit the King Von–Quando Rondo shooting, Lul Tim, YoungBoy, Savannah street politics, and the broader consequences of revenge, loyalty, and legal strategy in rap’s most closely watched cases.

--------
Comedian T.K. Kirkland sits down with DJ Vlad to unpack the fallout from Vlad’s public dispute with N.O.R.E. (Noreaga), including missed interview plans, comments made on Drink Champs, and Vlad’s response on Akademiks and social media. The conversation turns serious with the sexual assault lawsuit filed against N.O.R.E. over an alleged 1999 club incident, a claim both men stress has not been proven in court. Kirkland explains why accusations alone can threaten sponsorships, business deals, and long-term income, warning that such charges can damage your money before any verdict. Vlad also discusses pressure-to-drink claims involving DMX, Lamar Odom, and Kanye West’s Adidas controversy, while Kirkland reflects on humility, unforeseen consequences, judges, legal fees, public defenders, Michael Jackson settlements, Bill Cosby cases, and the risks celebrities face when personal beefs collide with the courts.

--------
Max B joins Vlad for a Harlem-focused “This or That” bracket, weighing legends and hometown favorites across generations of hip-hop. From Kool Moe Dee, Dougie Fresh and Big L to Ma$e, Cam’ron, A$AP Rocky, A$AP Ferg, Dave East, Jim Jones, Black Rob, G Dep, Diddy and Herb McGruff, the Wave God breaks down his picks with personal stories and sharp respect for Harlem’s rap legacy.

Along the way, Max reflects on writing for Chaze Bubs, contributing to the Purple Album, wanting Fergie Baby and Chase Benji on EMG, and linking with A$AP Rocky in the studio. He also speaks on Diddy’s impact through Bad Boy, recalls Herb McGruff’s music helping him through prison, and shares that Cam’ron once tried to help with bail. A candid, funny look at Harlem rap history from one of its most distinctive voices.

--------
In this VladTV interview, former Norteño shot caller Mario Sanchez reflects on prison, violence, addiction and the split-second decisions that can destroy a young man’s future. Responding to Vlad’s past interview with Clark Fredricks, Sanchez discusses how revenge, immaturity and life under the influence of drugs or alcohol put many men behind bars before their brains are fully developed. He also compares the violent prison culture of the 1990s with the drug-fueled crimes he saw after returning to jail in 2014.

Sanchez then addresses the decades-long conflict involving the Mexican Mafia and RF, arguing that Mexican and Mexican-American communities face bigger threats today. He says rival Mexican gangs should stop fighting each other and pay attention to ICE raids, deportations, Border Patrol activity and Latino agents targeting their own communities. Sanchez also mentions his new book, available September 15 on Amazon and Barnes & Noble.

recentItems.description:

https://www.youtube.com/vladtv/join
--------
Former Army Ranger sniper Nicholas Irving joins Shawn Prez on VladTV to discuss the ongoing Iran conflict, military intelligence, the reliability of government narratives, and growing concerns over national security.
Irving argues that prolonged wars can become a cycle of repeated headlines and shifting objectives that eventually exhaust public attention. Drawing comparisons to Afghanistan, he questions whether the U.S. has learned from past nation-building failures and warns that a ground invasion of Iran could become an even more difficult and costly conflict.
The conversation also examines claims that Iran could be close to developing a nuclear weapon. Irving expresses skepticism toward intelligence used to justify military action, pointing to past failures surrounding weapons of mass destruction in Iraq and questioning how much current intelligence is driven by legitimate security concerns versus political pressure.
Shawn and Nicholas also discuss conflicting accounts from Robert O'Neill and Matt Bissonnette regarding the mission that killed Osama bin Laden. Irving explains how the "fog of war" can cause members of the same operation to remember fast-moving combat events differently without necessarily meaning one account is intentionally false.
The discussion then turns to domestic politics, political rallies, government surveillance, and whether Americans are safer today than before 9/11. Irving argues that increased division and the possibility of coordinated domestic attacks present serious challenges, while also cautioning against jumping to conspiracy theories surrounding recent criminal investigations.

Interview by: Shawn Prez
